why: This run is not a measurement. It measured an app server that could not open new database connections, because the RDS-managed master secret had rotated 32 minutes earlier and the server's appserver.conf still held the previous password. The record is corrected additively; run-metadata.json is left exactly as the run wrote it.

actual.environment.cachePolicy: warm-after-900s-run, but against a server with a stale database credential

notMeasurement.reason: the database credential had rotated and the app server held the old one, so every new pooled connection failed with HTTP 500

basis: 40 of 3,396 requests failed (1.18%) against a recorded MAX_FAILED_PERCENT gate of 0.05%: 38 were HTTP 500, one 401, one premature close
the app server log carries `FATAL: password authentication failed for user "openchs"` and `Unable to acquire JDBC Connection` at 04:57:12Z, inside the run window
achieved 39.95 rps, BELOW the 90 s run's 43.00 -- a 75 s window cannot be slower than a 90 s one, which is what first showed the run was wrong rather than interesting
only 3,396 of 4,300 requests were issued, because a failed request ends that user's chain
the 900 s run immediately before it, on the same server after the same rotation, had zero failures: at ~1 device in flight it needed no new connection, so the fault is invisible at low concurrency
p95 was 403 ms and max 1,118 ms, so the server was not saturated -- these are errors, not queueing
cause: The loadtest RDS instance uses an AWS-managed master secret with RotationEnabled and a 7-day schedule. avni_server_db_password is read from Secrets Manager by the Makefile at playbook time and written into appserver.conf, so it is a point-in-time copy that a rotation silently invalidates. Connections already in the Hikari pool keep working, so /ping and /idp-details both returned 200 and the fault only appears when load forces the pool to grow.
keptBecause: The 75 s window still has not been measured; this run is kept as the record of why, and as evidence for a failure mode that applies to any environment using an AWS-managed RDS secret with a config-file copy of the password.
